summary: Right colour and bundle idea for orange UPVC sewer pipe, but black interiors, flat diagonal straps, flush identical ends and token bearers make it read as CG.
critique: Good: the terracotta-orange UPVC colour is right, the pipes are nested in offset layers, socket (bell) ends are modelled, and faint print runs along the barrels. Problems, in order of visibility: (1) Every pipe bore is a pure black void. Real UPVC is the same orange inside, a little lighter and glossier, with the darkness only a gradient a pipe-diameter or two deep. At three-quarter view the 12 black discs are the first thing you see and they read as holes in the mesh. (2) The straps are wrong. In the top views they are flat ribbons crossing the top face diagonally, like two planks laid in an X, not steel or poly bands wrapped round the bundle at right angles to the pipes. They have no thickness, no buckle or seal, and do not follow the curve of the pipes. (3) All pipes are the same length, perfectly flush, and all sockets point the same way. Real packs alternate socket ends layer by layer so the sockets nest, which leaves a staggered, toothed end profile. (4) There are three small timber blocks under the pack. Real 6 m packs sit in timber cassette frames (about 75x100 mm softwood, top and bottom, bolted through) every 1-1.5 m, or at least on full-width bearers. (5) The surface is spotless and evenly glossy: no mud, no scuffed lower pipes, no UV fading on top, no end caps, and the print is too faint to read even in the close view. (6) Pipe wall thickness at the spigot end looks very thin, around 3 mm on a roughly 160 mm pipe. SN4 160 mm is 4.7 mm and SN8 is 6.2 mm.
suggestions: Shade the bore: use the same orange albedo (about sRGB 190,90,40) inside, darkened by a baked AO gradient over 1-2 diameters into the pipe, with no pure black. This is an inner cylinder of about 12 segments with its normals flipped, or reuse the outer mesh at 0.94 scale with an inverted normal map. It costs nothing.

Replace the straps with real bands: a 19x0.6 mm flat loop that conforms to the outer hull of the bundle (a convex hull of the pipe circles, extruded), placed perpendicular to the pipe axis at each cassette frame, with a small seal block (20x30x8 mm). About 60-100 tris each.

Add timber cassette frames: two 75x100 mm rails (top and bottom) plus two vertical 75x75 mm posts with two M12 threaded rods, every 1.5 m (3-4 frames). About 300 tris per frame with a shared wood texture. Remove the three small blocks.
Alternate socket direction per layer and offset each pipe end by 0-60 mm at random, so the end face is staggered and the sockets nest.

Add wear: a mud and grass splash mask on the bottom 20 cm of the lowest layer, slight top-surface fade (desaturate the top layer by 10%), roughness from 0.35 to 0.5 with a fine scratch normal, and legible repeating ink-jet print ('BS EN 1401-1 160 SN4 ...') in black at about 8 mm text height every 1 m. Add red or black push-fit end caps on 2-3 random pipes.
Thicken the walls to about 5-6 mm with a chamfered spigot end, and make the socket outer diameter visibly larger (about +8%) with a short lead-in taper.
renderer_notes: Some of the black bore comes from the renderer having no GI or bounce, but the albedo or AO inside must still not be black. The lawn is a renderer backdrop.

summary: Correct proportions and parts (banded pole, spring base, ~0.5 m flag on a sleeve), but the flag reads as a smooth plastic sheet and the pole has no ground fitting or wear.
critique: Proportions match the Laws (post about 1.5 m, flag about 0.45-0.5 m square). The red and white banding, white top cap, sleeve with a ring at the flag foot, and black spring base are all the right parts. What keeps it at 'clearly CG': (1) The flag cloth is a smooth, evenly lit sheet with one soft bend. It has no fabric weave, hem stitching, double-stitched edge, or fly-edge fraying, and its sheen is uniform. In the side view it curls into a tube that looks like stiff vinyl. (2) The red is a slightly pink, over-saturated colour on both pole and flag, and it changes hue a lot between views (salmon in one, deep crimson in another), which suggests a very smooth, low-roughness red. (3) The pole is a perfectly straight, perfectly clean cylinder. Real corner posts have grass and mud stains on the bottom 20-30 cm, scuffs from boots and balls, and the bands are often vinyl tape with visible overlap seams. (4) The spring sits straight on the turf. It has no ground socket, collar or base cup, so the post appears to stand on the grass rather than in it. (5) The flag has no shadow or self-occlusion where the sleeve wraps the pole.
suggestions: Add a ground socket: a 40 mm black or white plastic collar (Ø 50 mm, 30 mm proud) under the spring, with a slight turf dip or ring around it (about 40 tris plus a small decal).

Flag material: add a tileable woven-polyester normal map (2-3 mm weave), roughness 0.6-0.7, slight transmission or backlit translucency if the shader allows (or brighten the backface by 15%), and a 10 mm double-stitched hem on the free edges via the normal map. Add 2-3 more wave folds along the fly edge, with the amplitude increasing away from the pole.
Lower the red saturation and raise its roughness: pole tape about sRGB 200,30,40 with roughness 0.45. Add tape-overlap seams (a 1 mm ridge in the normal map at each band joint).
Add wear: a grass and mud gradient on the bottom 25 cm of the pole and spring, 2-3 scuff marks on the white bands, and a faint grey grime at the flag's sleeve edge.
Give the pole a 2-3 degree lean or bend variant per instance (via a vertex shader or two mesh variants) so lines of corner flags do not look cloned.
renderer_notes: The hue shift between views is partly the sun and sky lighting, but it is exaggerated by the low roughness.

summary: Recognisable curved polycarbonate team shelter with tip-up seats, but the glazing has no presence, the frame is thin generic tube, and it lacks a floor, fixings and wear.
critique: Length (about 6 m, 10 seats), roof height (about 2.3 m) and the curved-canopy silhouette with a solid lower back panel match the common UK portable team shelter. What breaks it: (1) The polycarbonate has no reflections, edge thickness, tint or highlight. It is a faint green-grey veil, so from the back the shelter looks like an empty frame, and in the side view the canopy disappears. (2) The frame is about 4 thin round tubes bent into hoops plus top rails. Real shelters use 50x50 or 60x40 mm extruded aluminium box or oval sections with corner castings, a gutter or fascia profile along the front roof edge, and glazing bars at each sheet joint about every 1-1.5 m. (3) There is no floor and no base. Real shelters sit on an aluminium or plastic deck, an artificial-turf mat, or a concrete plinth, with ground anchors or wheel kits. Here the seats and panels stand straight on the grass. (4) The red panels are a flat, featureless colour with no panel joints, rivets, fixings or sponsor boards. 'HOME TEAM' is plain default-font text centred on the back. (5) The seats are a good shape but look pinkish-red and uniformly glossy. The seat rail and black legs are thin, with no feet or plates. There is no pedestal detail, no seat numbering and no padding. Most pro shelters use padded bucket seats, but a club or training-ground shelter is fine with plastic. (6) There is no wear: no scuffs on the kick panel, no grime in the polycarbonate channels, no water staining.
suggestions: Make the glazing visible: polycarbonate albedo of near-white at about 8% opacity, roughness 0.05, and a strong Fresnel or fake environment reflection, with a 10 mm visible edge thickness (a thin quad strip along every exposed sheet edge, slightly blue-grey). Add faint dirt or water-streak opacity at the bottom of each sheet via a shared 512 px grime mask.

Rebuild the frame from rectangular extrusions: 60x40 mm hoops at each 1.5 m bay (about 5 for 6 m), a front fascia or gutter profile (about 100 mm deep), and glazing bars on each sheet seam. Use a brushed aluminium material (albedo about 0.75, roughness 0.35) with a slight anodised tint. About 1.5k tris.
Add a base: a 50 mm aluminium deck or green artificial-turf mat across the full footprint, a 100x50 mm perimeter channel the panels sit in, and 4-6 ground-anchor plates. About 200 tris.

Detail the panels: vertical panel joints every 1.2 m with a 2 mm groove, rivet or bolt rows along the top and bottom edges (normal map), and an optional sponsor-board decal slot. Set the red to sRGB about 170,25,30 with roughness 0.5 and scuff marks on the lower 30 cm.

Seats: drop the pink cast (sRGB about 180,20,25), add a moulded drain hole and seat number decal, give the rail end plates or floor pedestals, and offer a padded-seat variant (about 400 tris per seat, instanced).
renderer_notes: Without screen-space reflections or an environment map the polycarbonate can't pick up reflections, so it may need a cheap fake reflection term in the asset material.

summary: A convincing construction-hoarding idea (printed face, studwork back, raking prop to kentledge) let down by clip-art graphics, crude studwork and a clean, floating base.
critique: This is one of the more thought-through props. It has a printed contractor face with a site-enquiries line and a Considerate Constructors badge, a paint-trim cap, stencilled panel numbers on the back, studs and rails, and a raking prop bolted to a concrete kentledge block with a metal shoe. A mud splash on the bottom of the face is a good touch. Weaknesses: (1) The face graphic is flat vector clip-art: cartoon trees, a cartoon building, and a perfectly uniform red field. Real hoarding wraps are photographic CGIs, and the vinyl shows sheet seams, slight sagging and creases, and reflective sheen. The single hairline vertical seam is good but too thin and perfect. (2) The panel is a lone 2.4 m square. Real site hoarding is a run of 1220x2440 mm ply sheets on 100x50 mm studs at 600 mm centres, with continuous 75x50 rails. The back here has only two widely spaced studs, and the rails seem to cross them in the same plane and slightly skewed, so the frame doesn't read as nailed timber. (3) The raking prop is a single thin timber at a steep angle meeting a small, pristine, perfectly cubic block. Real ones are 100x75 timber or steel props at about 45 degrees to 'Lego' concrete blocks or ballast-filled feet, chipped and dirty. (4) The panel meets the grass with no sole plate, no gap and no ground stain. The cap is a clean red extrusion. (5) The ply on the back is a uniform tan with no grain variation, no knots, no sheet-to-sheet tone shift and no weathering at the edges.
suggestions: Rebuild the back as real studwork: 100x50 mm studs at 600 mm centres (5 studs for 2.4 m), with 3 rails (bottom, mid and top) let into or fixed behind the studs. Give the ply 2 sheets with a 3 mm joint and a visible nail line every 150 mm (normal or albedo map). About 400 tris.

Face: make the vinyl graphic more photographic (a soft-shadowed CGI building, gradient sky, real-looking grass), and add a 2 m-wide sheet seam with 10 mm overlap, slight sheen variation (roughness 0.35 on vinyl versus 0.6 on painted ply edges), and faint creasing in the normal map near the seams.

Prop and kentledge: thicken the prop to 100x75, set it at about 45-55 degrees, and use a 0.8x0.4x0.4 m interlocking concrete block (studs on top) with chipped arrises, dirt and moss at the base, and a steel angle bracket with bolts. Add a second prop per 2.4 m panel or document it as half of a run.
Ground contact: add a 100x50 sole plate, a mud or grass-stain gradient on the lower 300 mm of both faces, and a few dandelions or long-grass cards at the base (shared foliage atlas).
Design it to tile: give the panel module 1220 mm-wide sheets with end studs flush, so runs of N panels join seamlessly and look like a continuous hoarding line.
renderer_notes: The long shadow and bright sky are lighting setup only.

summary: Correct parts (base plate, PTZ dome plus bullet camera, junction box, warning sign) on a pole that is too thin, untapered, clean and floating on a plate.
critique: Good inventory: a square bolted base plate, a mid-height section joint, a camera bracket with one PTZ dome and one bullet camera, a pole-mounted junction or PSU box, and a yellow 'CCTV' sign. At this distance it reads as a CCTV column. Issues: (1) The column is a constant small diameter top to bottom. A 6 m CCTV column has a root of about 140-160 mm, tapering or stepping to 76 mm at the top. Here it looks like about 90 mm throughout, so it looks like a scaffold tube. (2) The base is a thin flat plate sitting on the grass. Real columns are either planted (no plate, with a concrete collar or flush turf cut) or bolted to a raised concrete plinth with a bolt shroud or skirt over the nuts. (3) There is no inspection door. Real columns have a flush lockable door about 0.6-1.0 m above ground, about 400x100 mm, which is the most recognisable feature at eye level. (4) There is no cabling: no conduit or cable from the box up to the cameras, and no cable entry gland. (5) The galvanised finish is a clean, uniform light grey with no spangle, no darker weathered zones, no rust bloom at the base or welds, and no streaking. The camera housings are clean white with no sunshades or bird spikes. (6) The second camera bracket is a crude block, and the dome sits on a short stub. Real mounts use a swan-neck or wall-arm adaptor.
suggestions: Taper the shaft from 150 mm at the base to 76 mm at the top (or a stepped 2-section column with a swaged joint), with a 12-sided cross-section: the same tris as now.
Add a flush inspection door at 0.8 m: a 450x110 mm recessed panel with a lock (normal and albedo decal plus a 1 mm inset, about 20 tris).
Base: either a planted root with a 400 mm concrete collar ring flush with the turf, or a 600x600x150 mm concrete plinth with a 4-bolt grey plastic shroud (about 100 tris). Offer both as variants.

Material: a galvanised spangle detail texture (tileable 256 px), albedo about 0.55 with 10-15% variation, roughness 0.45-0.6, a darker oxidised gradient on the bottom 0.5 m and white zinc bloom streaks under the bracket. Add sticker or asset-tag decals.

Add an armoured cable or flexible conduit (Ø 20 mm, 6 sides, about 60 tris) from the junction box to each camera, and a sunshield hood on the bullet camera. Replace the block bracket with a proper swan-neck arm (bent tube, about 150 tris).
Add a small grime band where the column meets the ground, plus a few weed cards.
renderer_notes: The lawn and long shadow come from the scene setup.

summary: Believable columnar spruce silhouette with drooping branchlets, but the crown is see-through, the leader is spindly, and there are no dead lower branches or variation.
critique: The overall shape is a credible Norway spruce (narrow conical crown, height to spread about 5:1, pendulous secondary branches). The branch cards droop correctly in the close view, and the shadow is dense and organic. Issues: (1) The crown is too sparse and translucent. You can see the trunk through most of its height as a thin brown line, while a mature spruce is a near-opaque dark mass whose trunk is invisible above the first 2-3 m. (2) The top 15-20% is a bare stick with a few short twiggy cards and a dark knob at the tip. A spruce leader is a dense, upright, pointed spire with whorls of short branches. (3) The foliage colour is a fairly uniform mid-green with a slight blue cast. Norway spruce is much darker (sRGB about 35,60,40) with lighter, yellower new growth at the branch tips, and the interior should go almost black from self-shadow. (4) The bottom has a small brown mulch disc, with no lower dead branches, no sparse, browned lowest whorls, and no root flare. Real field-grown spruce often skirt to the ground, while woodland or stadium-edge trees have bare grey dead stubs on the bottom 2-4 m. (5) Branch whorls are not legible. Spruce has distinct tiers, each sweeping down and then curving up at the tips, and here the cards are evenly scattered. (6) The trunk is thin and reddish-brown with no bark texture visible.
suggestions: Increase crown density: about 1.5-2x the number of cards in the inner crown, plus a dark inner 'core' shell (a low-poly cone with dark needle albedo, about 200 tris) so the silhouette reads as solid and the trunk vanishes above 3 m.
Rebuild the leader: the top 2 m as a dense upright spire, 3-4 tight whorls of short upturned branch cards, and no bare stick. Remove the knob at the tip or make it a small cluster of cones.

Organise branches in whorls: 5-6 branches per tier, tiers every 0.4-0.6 m, each branch angled down 20-30 degrees and turning up at the tip, with pendulous branchlet cards hanging from it. Shorten tiers linearly toward the top.
Colour: needle albedo about sRGB 35,60,40, a yellow-green tip gradient (about 80,110,50) on the outer 10% of cards, and baked AO darkening toward the trunk to near-black.

Lower trunk: grey-brown scaly bark texture (512 px tileable), a root flare (widen the bottom 0.5 m by 30%), and 6-10 dead branch stubs or bare twig cards in the bottom 2-3 m. Swap the brown disc for needle litter blended into the grass.
Supply 3-4 seed variants plus an impostor or billboard LOD for distant rows. The full tree should stay under about 6-8k tris at LOD0 with a 1-2k LOD1.
renderer_notes: The bright, flat landscape and missing GI make the foliage look lighter than it would with proper occlusion. Some of the see-through look may be alpha-test LOD or MSAA thinning at distance.

summary: A plausible offset dish on a non-penetrating ballast frame with ribbed back and LNB arm, but the reflector, frame and ballast are clean, flat-shaded and under-detailed.
critique: Good structure: about a 1.2 m offset reflector with a rolled rim, 8 radial back ribs and a mounting plate with a label, an elevation and azimuth mast, a feed arm with LNB and bracket, diagonal stays down to a square steel non-penetrating frame, and 4 concrete ballast blocks. Issues: (1) The reflector face is a perfectly uniform off-white with a soft gradient. Real dishes have a slightly glossy painted steel or SMC surface with faint pressing ripples, a darker grimy bottom rim where water runs, and a bird-dropping or lichen patch. The 'SKYLINK' printed logo is good but too clean. The dish profile also looks very shallow, almost flat, from the side. (2) The feed arm is a thin straight tube. Real arms are square or C-section with a clamp collar at the dish and a moulded LNB holder, and a coax cable runs along the arm and down the mast to the ground. There is no cable here at all. (3) The mast and stays are thin uniform grey cylinders with no bolts, U-clamps or elevation scale plate. (4) The frame is plain square tube with flat ends. Real non-pen frames are galvanised C-channel with ballast trays, and they sit on rubber protection mats. (5) The ballast blocks are large, pristine, uniformly beige boxes. Real ones are 600x600x50 paving slabs stacked 2-4 high in trays, or proprietary concrete blocks, with chipped edges and staining. (6) The whole asset is spotless.
suggestions: Reflector: give it a real parabolic depth (f/D about 0.6, so a 1.2 m dish is about 75 mm deep at the centre), off-white paint (sRGB 225,225,220) with roughness 0.4, a subtle radial pressing normal map, and a grime gradient on the lower 20% and the rim lip. Keep the logo, but add slight wear.

Feed arm: change to a 40x40 mm square section with a clamp collar at the dish and a moulded LNB holder, plus a black coax cable (6-sided, Ø 7 mm) tied to the arm with 3 cable ties, running down the mast and off the frame. About 150 tris.
Mount detail: add U-bolt clamps, an elevation adjustment plate with a printed degree scale, nuts on every stay end, and galvanised spangle on all steel. Mast albedo about 0.5 with roughness 0.5.

Frame and ballast: model the frame as 41x41 mm C-channel (strut) with slotted holes (normal map), add ballast trays, and replace the blocks with stacked 600x600x50 slabs (2-3 per tray) with chipped edges, algae staining and slight misalignment. Add rubber mat pads under each foot.
Add a weathered variant (rust bleed at bolts, a lichen-spotted dish) for reuse on stadium roofs.
renderer_notes: The dish looks flat partly because there are no reflections and the sky ambient is soft. Grass is a staging backdrop.

summary: No stands or seating appear anywhere in either sheet; the layout is a bare pitch in open farmland.
critique: Neither the overall nor the detail sheet contains any seating, terracing or stand structure. All eight views show only the pitch, goals and a corner flag on a flat green plane, with farmland to the horizon. This scores as missing content. If 'desert' is meant to be a pitch-only layout (no stands), exclude this part from scoring. If it is meant to have stands, the stand generation failed for this layout, or produced geometry far outside the camera framing (see the giant shadow note).
suggestions: Check whether the desert layout config requests stands. If it does, trace why nothing was emitted, for example an empty side list, a zero row count, or a culled or out-of-bounds transform.
If the layout is meant to be pitch-only, label it as such in the review harness so the part isn't scored.

Investigate the huge linear shadow band crossing the whole landscape in overall views 1 and 2 and detail views 2 and 4. Something very tall and thin (a mis-scaled or mis-placed mast or roof member, perhaps hundreds of metres high) is casting it from beyond the pitch.
renderer_notes: The shadow band could also come from a sky or far-field object, but its sharp, straight shape suggests real geometry.

summary: No roof present in any view.
critique: No roof, canopy or roof structure is visible. The only possible trace is the very long straight shadow band crossing the landscape, which could come from a mis-placed, mis-scaled roof truss or mast far outside the frame. Scored as missing.
suggestions: Confirm whether the desert layout should have roofs. If yes, check the roof placement transform (the long shadow suggests geometry kilometres long or very high).
Add a QA assert that each requested part's bounds intersect the stadium footprint plus a margin.

critique: There is no exterior wall, concourse, cladding or turnstile block in any view. The pitch edge is a hard rectangular boundary that drops straight into farmland, with no perimeter wall, fence or apron. Scored as missing.
suggestions: If intentional, at least add a perimeter: a 1.1 m pitch-side barrier or a 2.4 m palisade fence, and a hard-standing or tarmac apron of 3-6 m around the pitch, so the site doesn't end at a hard grass edge.

summary: No floodlight masts or roof-mounted lamps visible (unless the giant shadow is a mis-placed mast).
critique: No floodlights appear in any view. The long dead-straight shadow that crosses the entire landscape from the horizon looks like the cast of a very tall thin mast, which suggests a floodlight pylon placed far outside the stadium or scaled up by orders of magnitude. Either way, nothing usable is in frame.
suggestions: Check the floodlight transform and scale for this layout. Find the caster of the long shadow (render a top-down view at 5 km).
For a pitch-only layout, offer 4 or 6 corner masts of 15-18 m (training-ground scale) as the default.
renderer_notes: The shadow band is visible from all directions, so it is real geometry, not a sky artefact.

summary: Correct markings and goal dimensions with nice goal-mouth wear, but the concentric-ring mowing pattern, flat featureless turf at mid-distance and abrupt pitch edge read as CG.
critique: The line markings are correct and crisp: halfway line, centre circle, penalty boxes, D arcs, penalty spots and corner arcs. The goals look like 7.32x2.44 m with box-frame stanchions and a white powder finish. The nets have a visible hexagonal mesh, and the worn bald patches in the six-yard boxes are a good realism cue. Problems: (1) The mowing pattern is concentric rings centred on the centre spot, reaching across the whole pitch. Almost every UK pitch uses straight stripes (lengthways, widthways or a checkerboard). Rings are a novelty and look procedural, and here they also run straight through the penalty areas. (2) At mid and long distance the turf is a flat, untextured green with a few blotchy lighter patches. Grass detail appears only close to the camera, so the pitch reads as a painted plane. (3) The pitch ends in a hard rectangle with the surround a different flat green. There is no run-off strip, no edge line of the grass plot, no drainage channel, no hard standing and no technical area. (4) The net hexagons are large and sparse, so from the side the net reads as a pattern on a transparent sheet rather than cord. The net has no sag, droop or depth variation, and the back and top net planes look rigidly flat. Real nets hang loose at the bottom, pegged with ground pegs or held down by a weighted chain. (5) The goal frame is clean, perfectly white tube with no ground sockets, net hooks or wear. (6) The lines are pure white and perfectly uniform. Real painted lines are slightly translucent with grass showing through, and slightly uneven in width.
suggestions: Default to straight mowing stripes: 5-6 m wide bands along the length (or a checkerboard variant), with the light and dark contrast driven by blade direction (alternate the normal tilt about 15 degrees) rather than albedo blotches. Keep rings as a rare option.

Add a mid-distance turf detail layer: a tileable 1-2 m grass macro texture blended in between 10 and 80 m, plus a 20-40 m low-frequency colour variation (5-8% hue and value), so the field doesn't go flat beyond the near zone.

Pitch surround: a 3-6 m run-off strip in the same grass, a 300 mm perimeter drainage channel or kerb, and a hard-standing apron. Blend the pitch edge so it doesn't show as a rectangle against the landscape.

Nets: use a smaller mesh (120 mm square or hex) with cord about 4 mm thick (a line-shaded or alpha-tested texture with anti-aliasing), add a sag to the back panel (lower the top-back corners by 50-100 mm and let the bottom bulge), and add net pegs or a ground chain plus net hooks on the frame every 300 mm.
Line paint: alpha about 0.85 with the grass normal kept, width varying ±5 mm, slight overspray softening at the edges.
Goal frame: add ground sockets or flush caps at the post bases, slight scuffing on the lower posts, and a darker grimy band where the net ties to the frame.
renderer_notes: The flat mid-distance turf is partly the renderer's distance LOD on the lawn shader. The haze and sky colour are scene settings. The giant shadow band across the landscape is an unexplained scene object (see the other stadium_desert parts).

summary: No dugouts, team shelters or players' tunnel present.
critique: Neither the halfway-line views nor the overall views show any dugouts, technical-area markings or tunnel. This is scored as missing. The standalone team_shelter asset exists in the kit, so even a pitch-only layout could place two shelters at the halfway line.
suggestions: Place two team_shelter instances about 5 m from the touchline, either side of the halfway line, with technical-area boxes marked 1 m from the shelter and extending 1 m beyond each end.
If the layout intentionally omits them, exclude this part from scoring.

summary: No perimeter advertising boards or screens present.
critique: There are no pitch-side LED or static boards, end-of-pitch 3D carpets, or scoreboard screens in any view. The pitch edge is bare grass. Scored as missing.
suggestions: Even for a minimal layout, place static perimeter boards (about 0.9-1.0 m high) 3-5 m behind the touchlines and goal lines, or document the layout as pitch-only so this part isn't scored.
